In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of early-life conditions and events on the risk of breast and other cancers.
the effects of energy restriction in early development on the risk of cancer, with the mechanism of action of these effects, and with the implications of this research for the prevention of cancer.
the role of early life events, possibly including intrauterine events, in the etiology of breast cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence of an increased risk of breast cancer in women with a history of breast feeding or lactation.

the evidence indicates that early life conditions, possibly extending back to the intrauterines stages of life, affect the incidence of breast cancer, that the mechanism of this effect appears to be through a decrease in the size of the mammary gland and, inferentially through a decrease in total number of stem cells in the ductal tree of the mammary glands, and that this effect may account for some of the epidemiologic findings that are not explained by other breast cancer risk factors.
the mammary gland mass at birth is an important determinant of risk of breast cancer in later life, but the mechanism is unknown.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a woman's breast cancer risk depends on the number of mammary ductal stem cells in the breast, and that this number is set in early life.
breast cancer is the most common cancer in women and the most common cause of cancer deaths in women.
breast cancer risk is increased by early life exposure to estrogen and that breast cancer risk decreases by early life exposure of estrogen to the mammary gland.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the number of stem cells in the breast is determined by the size of the breast.
breast cancer risk is affected by the total number of stem cells that are present in the breast.

the number of mammary stem cells in the breast determines the lifetime risk of breast cancer, and the risk is increased if the number of cells is high, as in women of Asian descent, or decreased if the number of stem cells is low, as in women who are energy restricted early in life, such as those in famine conditions.
